title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 4
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 original questions, with a reason for every answer choice and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, and a reason for every answer choice: why the right one is right and why each wrong one is wrong.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. في الآخر هتلاقي شرح لكل اختيار: ليه الصح صح وليه الغلط غلط. والنسبة اللي هتظهر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 4
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes per module (54 questions, 64 minutes). In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest questions, and Module 2 adapts to your performance on Module 1 (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Questions usually follow this order: Craft and Structure, Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, then Expression of Ideas. There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it.

questions.p: Ulugh Beg, the fifteenth-century ruler of Samarkand, was ______ patron of astronomy: he built a great observatory in the city and personally took part in the work of measuring the positions of about a thousand stars.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: an indifferent
a devoted
a reluctant
a secretive
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: Ulugh Beg built an observatory and took part in the measurements himself, so he was a "devoted" patron. "Indifferent" and "reluctant" contradict this active role, and nothing in the text suggests he was "secretive."
ce: Opposite of the text: a ruler who personally measured stars was not uninterested.
Correct: building an observatory and joining the measurements himself shows deep, active commitment.
Nothing suggests he was unwilling; he chose to do the work himself.
The text says nothing about hiding his work; a great observatory is the opposite of secret.

questions.p: Economist Hoda Nassar found that when a city's fish market began showing each morning's prices on a public screen, prices at different stalls ______: within a few weeks, the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive stall for the same fish had shrunk by more than half.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: fluctuated
soared
diverged
converged
questions.e: After the colon, the text says the gap between stalls shrank by more than half, so the prices "converged" (came closer together). "Diverged" is the opposite, and "fluctuated" and "soared" describe changes in price level, not a narrowing gap.
ce: "Fluctuated" means rose and fell irregularly; the text describes prices moving closer together, not swinging up and down.
The text is about the gap between stalls, not about all prices rising sharply.
Reversed: "diverged" means moved apart, but the gap shrank.
Correct: a shrinking gap between the cheapest and most expensive stalls means the prices moved closer together.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century.
The river does not hurry, nor delay;
It keeps the ______ pace it kept of old,
And carries, as it carried yesterday,
The patient silt, the sunlight, and the cold.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: frantic
uneven
borrowed
steady
questions.e: The river "does not hurry, nor delay" and carries things "as it carried yesterday," so its pace is "steady." "Frantic" contradicts "does not hurry," and "uneven" contradicts the poem's emphasis on an unchanging rhythm.
ce: Contradicts "does not hurry" and "patient."
The poem stresses sameness ("as it carried yesterday"), not irregular movement.
Nothing in the poem suggests the river's pace belongs to something else.
Correct: a river that neither hurries nor delays and moves as it did "of old" keeps a steady pace.

questions.p: Physicist Tarek Mansour's model of how sand flows through an hourglass is deliberately ______: it ignores the shapes of individual grains and the moisture in the air, treating the sand as a simple fluid so that its main behavior can be calculated by hand.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: comprehensive
simplified
inaccurate
experimental
questions.e: The model leaves out grain shapes and moisture on purpose so it can be calculated by hand, so it is "simplified." "Comprehensive" is the opposite, and "inaccurate" goes too far: the text says nothing about the model's results being wrong.
ce: Reversed: a comprehensive model would include details such as grain shape and moisture, which this one ignores.
Correct: leaving out details on purpose so the main behavior is easy to calculate is what a simplified model does.
The text never says the model gives wrong results; leaving out details is not the same as being wrong, and no scientist makes a model "deliberately" wrong.
Nothing suggests the model is new or untested; the text is about what it leaves out.

questions.p: On Roda Island in Cairo stands a Nilometer built in the ninth century: a stone-lined shaft connected to the river, with a marked column at its center. Each summer, officials read the height that the floodwater reached on the column. The reading mattered far beyond the riverbank. A high flood meant well-watered fields and a large harvest, so the government used the measurement to set the taxes that farmers would owe that year.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that the Nilometer was the most important building in medieval Cairo
To compare the Nilometer with other methods of predicting the Nile's flood
To explain how a structure used to measure the Nile's flood also helped determine farmers' taxes
To describe how farmers dug canals to share the floodwater among their fields
questions.e: The text describes how the Nilometer worked and then explains why its reading "mattered far beyond the riverbank": it was used to set taxes. Calling it "the most important building" is an argument the text never makes, and no other flood-measuring methods are compared.
ce: The text makes no comparison with other buildings and makes no such argument.
No other method is mentioned.
Correct: the text describes the Nilometer and then shows how its reading was used to set taxes.
Canals are never mentioned; the farmers appear only as taxpayers.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original play. MARWAN, a merchant, has just learned that his ship has returned safely.
MARWAN: Safe! All of it safe—the silk, the pepper, the crew. (He sits, then stands again.) __Fetch the ledger. No, fetch my coat. No—__ (laughing) fetch nothing. Let me only stand here a moment and be a man whose ship came home.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
c: It shows that Marwan's excitement makes him unable to settle on a single action.
It reveals that Marwan distrusts the servants who work for him.
It suggests that Marwan doubts that the news about his ship is true.
It shows Marwan carefully planning how to sell the goods on his ship.
questions.e: Marwan gives one order, replaces it, and then drops both with a laugh, and the stage direction ("He sits, then stands again") adds to the picture of a man too excited to settle. He clearly believes the news ("Safe!"), so the idea that he doubts it is wrong.
ce: Correct: he changes his order twice in a row and then laughs, which shows joyful confusion.
He gives orders and then cancels them out of excitement; nothing suggests distrust.
He repeats "Safe!" and wants to enjoy being "a man whose ship came home," so he believes the news.
His orders are changed at once and then dropped; this is the opposite of careful planning.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many economists warn against price ceilings, which are legal limits on how much sellers may charge. When a ceiling holds a price below the level at which supply and demand would meet, buyers want more of the good than sellers are willing to offer, and shortages follow.

Text 2
Economist Samir Haddad studied a coastal town that capped the price of bottled water for ten days after a major storm. Shops there did not run out of water more often than shops in a nearby town with no cap. Haddad suggests that because sellers knew the cap would soon end, few of them held back stock or left the market. A short, clearly limited cap, he argues, may not cause the shortages that a long-lasting one would.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Haddad (Text 2) most likely respond to the warning in Text 1?
c: He would reject the warning completely, arguing that price ceilings never cause shortages.
He would agree with the warning, pointing to the shortages that followed the cap in the town he studied.
He would suggest that the warning may apply more to long-lasting price ceilings than to brief ones with a known end date.
He would argue that bottled water is not an essential good, so the warning does not apply to it.
questions.e: Haddad's study found no extra shortages under a brief cap, and he contrasts this with "a long-lasting one," so he would limit the warning rather than reject it. Saying ceilings "never" cause shortages is too extreme, since he still expects long caps to cause them.
ce: Too extreme: Haddad accepts that a long-lasting cap could cause shortages.
Contradicts Text 2: the capped town did not run out of water more often.
Correct: Haddad says a short, clearly limited cap "may not cause the shortages that a long-lasting one would."
Haddad never discusses whether water is essential; his point is about how long the cap lasts.

questions.p: The Moon takes the same amount of time to spin once on its axis as it does to orbit Earth, about 27 days. As a result, the same side of the Moon always faces Earth. This match is not a coincidence. Billions of years ago the Moon spun faster, but Earth's gravity stretched the Moon slightly, raising bulges in its rock. Earth's pull on these bulges acted like a brake, gradually slowing the Moon's spin until it matched the Moon's orbit, a state that astronomers call tidal locking.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: The Moon does not spin on its axis at all, which is why only one side of it can be seen from Earth.
Earth's gravity raises tides in Earth's oceans that are gradually slowing Earth's own spin.
The Moon shows only one side to Earth because Earth's gravity slowed the Moon's spin until it matched the time the Moon takes to orbit Earth.
The far side of the Moon has never been studied because it never faces Earth.
questions.e: The text explains why one side of the Moon always faces Earth: Earth's gravity braked the Moon's spin until it matched its orbit. The claim that the Moon does not spin misreads the first sentence, which says it spins once every 27 days.
ce: Contradicts the text: the Moon does spin, once every 27 days.
The text is about bulges in the Moon's rock and the Moon's spin, not Earth's oceans or Earth's spin.
Correct: this joins the fact (one side always faces Earth) with the explanation the text gives (Earth's gravity slowed the spin).
The text says nothing about whether the far side has been studied.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century. The speaker addresses a lamp.
Small lamp, you never boasted of your light,
Nor envied stars their larger share of sky;
You only kept one room against the night,
And kept it well, and let the hours go by.
The scholar read, the mother sewed, by you,
And no one praised the work you helped them do.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: The speaker complains that the lamp gives too little light to be useful.
The speaker praises the lamp for quietly doing useful work without seeking recognition.
The speaker suggests that the lamp is less valuable than the stars.
The speaker regrets that the scholar and the mother could not finish their work.
questions.e: The poem admires the lamp's modest, faithful service: it never boasted, kept one room "well," and helped others although "no one praised" it. The stars are mentioned only to show the lamp's lack of envy, not to rank the lamp below them.
ce: The speaker says the lamp kept the room "well" and helped the scholar and the mother, so it was useful.
Correct: the lamp "never boasted," "kept it well," and helped others' work although "no one praised" it.
The lamp did not envy the stars, but the poem honors the lamp rather than ranking it below them.
Nothing suggests their work was left unfinished; the lamp helped them do it.

questions.p: In 132 CE, the Chinese scholar Zhang Heng presented the Han court with a bronze instrument designed to register earthquakes. Eight dragons faced outward around the vessel, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad; when the ground shook, a ball was supposed to drop. Some historians argue that the device could sense earthquakes so distant that no one near it felt any shaking.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historians' argument?
c: Officials at the court reported feeling strong shaking on the same day that a ball dropped.
A record describes a ball dropping on a day when no shaking was felt at the court, followed days later by news of an earthquake in a distant region.
Modern copies of the instrument drop a ball when they are shaken firmly by hand.
The instrument was made of bronze, a metal widely used by craftsmen of the Han dynasty.
questions.e: The argument is that the device sensed quakes too far away to be felt, so the best support is a ball dropping with no local shaking, followed by news of a distant quake. Strong shaking felt at the court is the trap: it fits any working detector and says nothing about unfelt, distant quakes.
ce: Shaking felt nearby does not show that the device could detect earthquakes that people could not feel.
Correct: the device reacted although no one nearby felt anything, and the cause turned out to be a distant earthquake.
This shows only that strong shaking moves the balls, not that distant, unfelt earthquakes could.
The material says nothing about how sensitive the device was.

questions.p: In an original play, the character Layla is a young poet. In one scene, another character remarks that Layla cares more about the sound of her lines than about their meaning.
questions.q: Which quotation from the play most effectively illustrates this remark?
c: LAYLA: "I write every morning before the rest of the house wakes up."
LAYLA: "My teacher says a poem must first be true, and I believe him."
LAYLA: "Who cares what it says? Listen to how it rings—'silver,' 'silence,' 'sail'—the words chime like bells!"
LAYLA: "I have filled three notebooks this year, and I mean to fill a fourth."
questions.e: Only one line shows Layla brushing aside meaning while admiring how her words sound. The line about a poem being "true" suggests the opposite value, and the other lines describe her habits, not her priorities.
ce: This shows her routine, not what she values in a line.
Reversed: this puts truth (meaning) first.
Correct: she dismisses meaning ("Who cares what it says?") and delights only in sound ("rings," "chime").
This shows how much she writes, not whether she values sound over meaning.

questions.p:
Change in price and in quantity sold at one market over a month
Product | Change in price | Change in quantity sold
Bread | +10% | −2%
Strawberries | +10% | −18%
Rice | +10% | −3%
Chocolate | +10% | −15%

Economists say that demand for a good is inelastic when a rise in its price causes only a small fall in the quantity people buy, often because the good is a necessity. Examining data from one market, a student claims that the staple foods in the table, bread and rice, had more inelastic demand than the other two products.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?
c: After the same 10% price rise, the quantity of bread sold fell by only 2% and of rice by only 3%, while sales of strawberries and chocolate fell by 18% and 15%.
Strawberries showed the largest fall in quantity sold, 18%.
All four products rose in price by the same amount, 10%.
The quantity of rice sold fell by 3%, slightly more than the fall for bread.
questions.e: The claim compares bread and rice with the other two products, so the data must show small falls (2%, 3%) beside large ones (18%, 15%) after the same price rise. The other true statements describe a single product or compare the wrong pair.
ce: Correct: it compares the small falls for the staples with the large falls for the other products after the same price rise.
True, but it gives only one product and does not compare the staples with the others.
True, but it says nothing about how buyers responded, which is what elasticity measures.
True, but it compares the two staples with each other instead of with the other products.

questions.p:
Dips in brightness recorded for four stars of similar size
Star | Depth of dip (% of the star's light) | Time between dips (days)
Star H | 0.8 | 3.2
Star J | 0.1 | 45.0
Star K | 1.2 | 12.0
Star L | 0.4 | 7.0

When a planet passes in front of its star, the star's light dims slightly. For stars of similar size, a larger planet blocks more light and produces a deeper dip. Using data from four stars, a student claims that the planet orbiting Star K is the largest of the four planets.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?
c: Star J had the longest time between dips, 45 days.
Star H's dips came every 3.2 days, more often than those of any other star.
Star L's dip of 0.4% was deeper than Star J's dip of 0.1%.
The dip in Star K's light, 1.2%, was deeper than the dip recorded for any other star in the table.
questions.e: The text says a deeper dip means a larger planet, so Star K's 1.2% dip, the deepest in the table, supports the claim. The choices about time between dips use the wrong column, and the comparison of Star L with Star J leaves out Star K.
ce: Time between dips relates to the orbit, not to the planet's size.
How often dips occur does not show how large the planet is.
True, but it compares two other stars and says nothing about Star K.
Correct: the text links planet size to dip depth, and Star K's dip is the deepest.

questions.p: In the early eleventh century, the scholar al-Biruni estimated the size of Earth using a method that required only one location. From the top of a mountain of known height, he measured how far below the horizontal the horizon appeared, and then used geometry to calculate Earth's radius. An earlier measurement, made for the caliph al-Mamun in the ninth century, had required teams to travel across a flat plain and measure the distance they covered. Al-Biruni's method therefore ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: proved that the measurement made for al-Mamun had been wrong.
could be used only on flat plains like the one crossed by the earlier teams.
spared him the need to travel and measure a long distance on the ground.
required a larger team than the measurement made for al-Mamun.
questions.e: The contrast is between one location and teams traveling across a plain, so al-Biruni avoided measuring a long distance on the ground. Nothing compares the accuracy of the two results, so "proved … wrong" has no support.
ce: The text never compares the results of the two measurements.
Reversed: his method needed a mountain, not a flat plain.
Correct: his method needed one spot on a mountain, unlike the earlier method, which required teams to cover and measure a long distance.
The text suggests the opposite: one location versus traveling teams.

questions.p: Venus rotates in the opposite direction from most planets in the solar ______ on Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: system,
system
system;
system, and,
questions.e: "Venus rotates … solar system" and "on Venus, the Sun rises … east" are both independent clauses, so a semicolon joins them. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and no punctuation makes a run-on.
ce: Comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Run-on: two complete sentences with no punctuation between them.
Correct: both parts are complete sentences, and a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses.
The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

questions.p: The astrolabe, an instrument that let medieval astronomers and travelers measure the height of the Sun and stars above the ______ was refined by scholars across the Islamic world.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: horizon;
horizon—
horizon
horizon,
questions.e: "An instrument … horizon" is extra information about the astrolabe that begins with a comma, so it must end with a matching comma before the verb "was." A dash does not match the opening comma, and a semicolon separates the subject from its verb.
ce: A semicolon would cut the subject "The astrolabe" off from its verb "was."
A dash cannot close extra information that opened with a comma; the pair must match.
Without a closing comma, the extra information never ends, and "horizon was refined" reads as if the horizon was refined.
Correct: the extra information opens with a comma after "astrolabe," so it must close with a comma before "was."

questions.p: Ancient Egyptian scribes worked with simple tools that fit into a small ______ a palette, reed brushes, and cakes of black and red ink.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: kit;
kit, including:
kit
kit:
questions.e: "Ancient Egyptian scribes worked with simple tools that fit into a small kit" is a complete sentence, and a list follows, so a colon is correct. A semicolon needs a full clause on both sides, and a colon cannot come straight after "including."
ce: A semicolon needs a complete sentence after it, but "a palette, reed brushes, and cakes … ink" is only a list.
A colon must follow a complete sentence; "including" leaves the sentence unfinished before the colon.
With no punctuation, "kit a palette" runs the list into the sentence and makes no sense.
Correct: a complete sentence comes before the list, so a colon introduces it.

questions.p: The pulsar discovered by astronomers Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in ______ appeared in their data as a series of radio pulses arriving roughly every 1.3 seconds.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The whole phrase "The pulsar discovered by … in 1967" is the subject of "appeared," so no punctuation belongs between them. A comma, semicolon, or dash would split the subject from its verb.
ce: A single comma between the subject and the verb "appeared" is never correct.
A semicolon would leave "The pulsar discovered … in 1967" as a fragment.
Correct: "The pulsar discovered … in 1967" is the subject, and no punctuation may separate a subject from its verb "appeared."
A single dash wrongly separates the subject from its verb; there is no extra information to set off.

questions.p: The collection of clay tablets found in the palace archives of an ancient Syrian city ______ records of grain, wool, and oil delivered to the royal storehouses.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: contain
contains
are containing
have contained
questions.e: Ignore the phrases "of clay tablets" and "found in the palace archives…": the subject is "collection," which is singular, so "contains" is correct. The other choices are plural forms that match the nearby nouns "tablets" and "archives."
ce: Plural verb: it agrees with "tablets" or "archives," not with the real subject, "collection."
Correct: the subject is the singular noun "collection," so it needs the singular verb "contains."
Plural, and "contain" is not normally used in the -ing form to describe what something holds.
Plural verb that does not agree with the singular subject "collection."

questions.p: The Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō set out on foot through northern Japan in 1689, and that journey inspired one of the ______ best-known works, a travel diary that mixes prose with haiku.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: poets
poets'
poet's
poet's'
questions.e: The works belong to one poet, Bashō, so the singular possessive "poet's" is correct. "Poets'" would mean several poets, and "poets" is a plain plural that shows no ownership.
ce: Plural with no apostrophe: it does not show possession.
Plural possessive: it would mean the works belong to several poets, but only Bashō is meant.
Correct: one poet (Bashō) owns the works, so the singular possessive "poet's" is needed.
Not a standard English form.

questions.p: By the time the Song dynasty government took control of printing paper money in the region of Sichuan in the early 1020s, merchants there ______ their own paper notes for years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: had been issuing
will issue
are issuing
issue
questions.e: "By the time" + a past event signals an action already under way before that moment, so "had been issuing" is correct. "Will issue," "are issuing," and "issue" are future or present forms that clash with the past time frame.
ce: Correct: the merchants' issuing began earlier and continued up to a past moment ("By the time … took control"), so the past perfect progressive is needed.
Future tense cannot describe actions that happened before a past event.
Present tense does not fit a sentence about the 1020s.
Present tense; it also loses the idea of an action that came before another past action.

questions.p: To the naked eye, most stars look whitish. ______ a few, such as Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion, have a clearly reddish color.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Therefore,
For example,
Similarly,
However,
questions.e: The first sentence states a general pattern and the second gives exceptions, so a contrast word, "However," fits. "For example" would wrongly present the red star as an illustration of white stars.
ce: The reddish stars are not a result of most stars looking white.
Betelgeuse is not an example of a whitish star; it is an exception.
The second sentence describes a difference, not something similar.
Correct: a few reddish stars contrast with the general rule that most stars look whitish.

questions.p: When a ride-hailing app raises its fares during periods of heavy demand, more drivers tend to start working in order to earn the higher pay. ______ riders who are willing to pay the higher fare find a car more quickly, while some others decide to wait or to walk instead.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Nevertheless,
Similarly,
In contrast,
As a result,
questions.e: Higher fares bring more drivers, and more drivers mean faster rides for those who pay, so "As a result" shows the cause-and-effect link. "Nevertheless" and "In contrast" wrongly signal an opposing idea.
ce: There is no contrast: finding a car more quickly is the expected effect of more drivers.
The second sentence describes a consequence, not a similar situation.
The riders' experience follows from the first sentence instead of opposing it.
Correct: more drivers on the road leads to riders finding cars faster, so a cause-and-effect transition fits.

questions.p: The ancient Egyptian civil calendar had 365 days: twelve months of thirty days each, plus five extra days at the end of the year. Because the true solar year is about a quarter of a day longer, the calendar slowly drifted out of step with the seasons. ______ over the centuries, festivals that had once fallen in summer came to be celebrated in other seasons.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Consequently,
In contrast,
Previously,
Nonetheless,
questions.e: The drift described in the second sentence causes the festivals to move, so "Consequently" fits. "Nonetheless" would suggest that the festivals moved in spite of the drift, which reverses the logic.
ce: Correct: festivals moving to other seasons is the result of the calendar drifting.
The festivals moving is not opposed to the drift; it is caused by it.
The festivals moved after the drift began, not before it.
"Nonetheless" signals something unexpected, but the festivals moving is exactly what the drift would cause.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Zheng He was a Chinese admiral of the Ming dynasty.
• Between 1405 and 1433, he led seven large voyages across the Indian Ocean.
• His fleets visited ports in Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa.
• The ships carried goods and gifts such as silk and porcelain.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the geographic reach of Zheng He's voyages. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Zheng He was a Chinese admiral of the Ming dynasty who led seven voyages.
Zheng He's seven voyages, made between 1405 and 1433, took his fleets to ports as far apart as Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa.
Zheng He's ships carried goods and gifts such as silk and porcelain.
Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven large voyages.
questions.e: Geographic reach means how far the voyages went, so the sentence must list the distant regions: Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa. The other choices give true details (rank, cargo, dates) that do not show reach.
ce: It introduces Zheng He but says nothing about where the voyages went.
Correct: it names the wide range of regions the fleets reached, which is what "geographic reach" means.
This is about the cargo, not the places reached.
This gives dates and number, not geographic reach.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Al-Jazari was an engineer who worked in the region of the upper Tigris River.
• In 1206, he completed a book describing about fifty mechanical devices.
• One device, the "elephant clock," measured time using a bowl that slowly sank in water.
• The book included detailed drawings showing how to build each device.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce al-Jazari's book to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Completed in 1206 by the engineer al-Jazari, the book describes about fifty mechanical devices and includes detailed drawings showing how to build each one.
Al-Jazari's elephant clock measured time using a bowl that slowly sank in water.
Al-Jazari was an engineer who worked in the region of the upper Tigris River.
The elephant clock is one of about fifty devices.
questions.e: An introduction to the book for new readers needs its author, date, and contents, which only the sentence about fifty devices and their drawings provides. The elephant-clock choices focus on a single device, and the sentence about the upper Tigris introduces the man rather than the book.
ce: Correct: it says who wrote the book, when, what it contains, and how it presents the devices.
This describes one device, not the book as a whole.
This introduces the engineer, not the book.
It names one device and a number but never explains what the book is or who wrote it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1970, economist George Akerlof published a paper about markets in which sellers know more than buyers.
• His main example was the market for used cars.
• Buyers who cannot tell good cars from bad ones offer only an average price.
• Owners of good cars may then refuse to sell, so mostly poor-quality cars are left for sale.
questions.q: The student wants to explain why good cars may disappear from the market, according to Akerlof. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: According to Akerlof, buyers who cannot tell good cars from bad ones offer only an average price, so owners of good cars may refuse to sell, leaving mostly poor-quality cars for sale.
In 1970, Akerlof published a paper about markets in which sellers know more than buyers.
Akerlof's main example was the market for used cars.
According to Akerlof, mostly poor-quality cars may be left for sale in the used-car market.
questions.e: The goal is to explain why, so the sentence needs the cause (buyers offer only an average price) and the effect (good-car owners stop selling). The choice that mentions only poor-quality cars being left gives the result without the reason.
ce: Correct: it gives the cause (average offers) and the effect (good cars leave the market).
It introduces the paper but does not explain why good cars disappear.
It names the example but gives no explanation.
It states the result but leaves out the reason, which the goal asks for.

questions.p: Historians once treated the scholars of the Maragha observatory, founded in northwestern Iran in 1259, as mere ______ of ancient Greek astronomy. Closer study of their work shows that they did far more: they proposed new geometrical models to fix problems they had found in Ptolemy's system.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: challengers
founders
detractors
preservers
questions.e: "Mere" signals a small role that the second sentence corrects ("they did far more"), so historians had seen them only as "preservers" of Greek astronomy. "Challengers" describes what the scholars actually did, so it cannot be the older, mistaken view.
ce: The text says the scholars did challenge Ptolemy, so historians who saw them as "mere challengers" would not be corrected by this evidence.
"Mere founders" makes no sense; founding a field would not be a small role.
Calling them "mere detractors" (critics) does not fit the contrast; the evidence shows they built new models, not that they kept old ones.
Correct: "mere preservers" means people who only kept old knowledge alive, the limited role that "did far more" corrects.

questions.p: Economist Lina Fares argues that the popularity of "flash sales," discounts that last only an hour or two, does not depend chiefly on the size of the discount. Instead, she contends, such sales succeed by creating a sense of ______: shoppers fear that if they pause to compare prices, the offer will be gone.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: urgency
complacency
solidarity
deliberation
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: shoppers rush because the offer may vanish, which is "urgency." "Deliberation" is the slow comparing that flash sales discourage, and "complacency" is the opposite feeling.
ce: Correct: fearing that the offer will disappear if they pause is a feeling of urgency.
Reversed: complacency means feeling relaxed and satisfied, the opposite of rushing.
Solidarity means unity with a group; the text describes individual fear of missing an offer.
Deliberation means careful thought, which is exactly what shoppers avoid when they do not pause to compare.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century.
He wrote his verses on the sand at noon,
And smiled to see the tide erase them soon;
He did not mourn them, for he held it true
That words, like waves, were ______, and ever new.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: permanent
bitter
costly
fleeting
questions.e: The verses are quickly erased and the speaker compares words to waves, so words are "fleeting," but always replaced ("ever new"). "Permanent" contradicts the tide erasing the lines, and "bitter" clashes with his smile.
ce: Contradicts the image of the tide erasing his verses.
He "did not mourn them" and smiled, so nothing in the poem is bitter.
Nothing suggests that words cost him anything; he lets them go easily.
Correct: like waves and like verses erased by the tide, words pass quickly, yet they are "ever new."

questions.p: Physicists describe the Leidenfrost effect as ______: a drop of water on a pan heated far above water's boiling point lasts longer than a drop on a pan only slightly above it, because a thin layer of vapor forms beneath the hotter drop and shields it from the metal.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: negligible
predictable
counterintuitive
hazardous
questions.e: The example after the colon is surprising: the drop survives longer on the hotter pan, so the effect is "counterintuitive." "Predictable" misses that surprise, and "negligible" contradicts the clear difference the text describes.
ce: The effect makes a clear difference in how long a drop lasts, so it is not too small to matter.
The point of the example is that the result is surprising, not what one would expect.
Correct: a drop lasting longer on a hotter pan goes against what most people would expect.
Nothing in the text discusses danger.

questions.p: Astronomers cannot travel to a distant star to measure how it is moving. Instead, they examine its light. When a star moves toward Earth, the light waves reaching us are squeezed together slightly, shifting the dark lines in the star's spectrum toward the blue end; when it moves away, the waves are stretched and the lines shift toward the red. By measuring the size of this shift, astronomers can calculate how fast the star is approaching or moving away.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the overall structure of the text?
c: It identifies a limitation that the method described in the rest of the text allows astronomers to overcome.
It introduces a claim that the rest of the text argues is mistaken.
It presents a hypothesis that the final sentence confirms.
It describes the result of a measurement explained in the following sentences.
questions.e: The first sentence states a problem (stars are out of reach), and the rest explains the method that solves it ("Instead, they examine its light"). Nothing later disputes that sentence, so it is not a claim shown to be mistaken.
ce: Correct: astronomers cannot reach stars, so they use the light-shift method that the rest of the text explains.
The text never disputes the first sentence; it works around it.
The first sentence is a fact about a limitation, not a hypothesis to be tested.
It describes what astronomers cannot do, not the result of any measurement.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original play. Two brothers, HASSAN and YOUSSEF, are dividing their late father's belongings.
HASSAN: Take the clock. You always wound it.
YOUSSEF: I wound it because he asked me to. You were the one who sat and listened to it.
HASSAN: (after a pause) Then we'll leave it where it is. Let it keep his time a little longer.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: One brother demands an object, the other refuses to give it up, and they agree to sell it.
One brother offers an object to the other, the second brother suggests that the first is more attached to it, and the first decides that neither of them should take it.
Both brothers describe their father's habits and then argue about how much the clock is worth.
One brother criticizes the way the other treated their father, and the second brother apologizes.
questions.e: The exchange moves from an offer ("Take the clock") to Youssef's reply that Hassan valued it more, to Hassan's decision to leave it where it is. There is no demand, sale, argument about money, or apology.
ce: Hassan offers the clock instead of demanding it, and no sale is mentioned.
Correct: Hassan offers the clock, Youssef turns the offer back, and Hassan decides to leave it in place.
Money is never discussed, and the brothers do not argue about value.
Nobody criticizes or apologizes; each brother links the clock to the other.

questions.p:
Text 1
In some experiments, containers of hot water placed in a freezer have frozen before identical containers of cooler water, a result known as the Mpemba effect. Researchers who report the effect have proposed explanations such as faster evaporation from the hot water, which leaves less water to freeze.

Text 2
Physicist Clara Novak repeated freezing experiments while carefully controlling where the containers sat in the freezer, where the thermometers were placed, and the exact moment counted as "frozen." Under these controls, the hot water never froze first. Novak concludes that many reported cases may reflect differences in how the experiments were set up and measured rather than a real effect of the starting temperature.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Novak (Text 2) most likely respond to the researchers discussed in Text 1?
c: She would agree that faster evaporation explains why hot water froze first in her own experiments.
She would argue that the results they try to explain may come from uncontrolled differences in how experiments were run, so the effect itself may not need explaining.
She would argue that hot water always freezes more slowly than cooler water under any possible conditions.
She would suggest that the effect appears only when containers are placed close together in the freezer.
questions.e: Novak questions whether there is a real effect at all, so she would say the researchers may be explaining something caused by uncontrolled set-ups. The claim that hot water "always" freezes more slowly "under any possible conditions" goes beyond her cautious conclusion.
ce: In her experiments, the hot water never froze first.
Correct: Novak suggests the reported cases may reflect set-up and measurement differences rather than a real effect.
Too extreme: she tested only her controlled conditions and says reported cases "may" reflect set-up differences.
She controlled placement but never claims that placement alone produces the effect.

questions.p: After a bloody war against the kingdom of Kalinga around 261 BCE, the Indian emperor Ashoka had messages carved on rocks and stone pillars across his empire. Rather than celebrating his victories, many of these edicts urge respect for parents and teachers, tolerance between religious groups, and kindness toward animals. Written in local languages and scripts, the edicts were placed along roads and near towns, where officials could read them aloud to people who could not read.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Ashoka's edicts mainly record the details of his military victory over Kalinga.
Ashoka used inscriptions placed throughout his empire to spread moral teachings among his subjects.
Ashoka required his officials to teach his subjects to read local scripts.
Ashoka's edicts were all carved in a single language understood across the empire.
questions.e: The text is about edicts that spread moral messages (respect, tolerance, kindness) to people across the empire. The choice about recording military victories reverses "Rather than celebrating his victories," and the single-language choice contradicts "local languages and scripts."
ce: Contradicts the text: the edicts urge respect and kindness "rather than celebrating his victories."
Correct: the text explains what the edicts taught and how they were placed so people could hear them.
Officials read the edicts aloud; nothing says they taught reading.
Contradicts the text: they were written in "local languages and scripts."

questions.p:
The following text is from an original poem written in the style of the nineteenth century. The speaker describes an old astronomer.
He charted every star the seasons brought,
But kept no diary of his own long years;
His notebooks hold the heavens, every thought,
And not one line about his joys or fears.
questions.q: According to the text, what is true about the astronomer's notebooks?
c: They contain a diary of his long life and work.
They were lost before he could finish charting the stars.
They describe his joys and fears about his discoveries.
They record his observations of the sky but say nothing about his personal life.
questions.e: The notebooks are full of the sky ("hold the heavens") but contain "not one line about his joys or fears," so they leave out his personal life. The diary choice contradicts "kept no diary," and the joys-and-fears choice contradicts the last line.
ce: Contradicts the poem: he "kept no diary of his own long years."
Nothing suggests the notebooks were lost; he charted "every star."
Contradicts "not one line about his joys or fears."
Correct: they "hold the heavens" but have "not one line about his joys or fears."

questions.p: Economist Nabil Sabry studied farmers' markets in which several stalls sell nearly identical tomatoes. He hypothesizes that when such stalls stand side by side, so that shoppers can compare prices at a glance, sellers keep their prices closer together than they do when the stalls are spread across the market.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sabry's hypothesis?
c: Shoppers at all of the markets said that price was the most important factor when buying tomatoes.
In markets where tomato stalls stood next to one another, the gap between the highest and lowest tomato prices was much smaller than in markets where the stalls were far apart.
Tomato prices at every market rose during the winter, when fewer tomatoes were harvested.
Stalls placed side by side sold more tomatoes in total than stalls that were spread out.
questions.e: Sabry predicts smaller price differences when stalls are side by side, so a finding of a much smaller price gap in those markets supports him directly. Higher total sales for side-by-side stalls is the tempting trap, but sales volume is not what the hypothesis is about.
ce: This does not compare side-by-side stalls with spread-out stalls.
Correct: it compares price gaps under the two layouts, exactly what the hypothesis predicts.
A general price rise says nothing about how close prices were to each other under different layouts.
The hypothesis is about how close prices are, not how many tomatoes were sold.

questions.p:
Rotation and orbit times of four planets around the star Kepra
Planet | Time to rotate once (Earth days) | Time to orbit the star once (Earth days)
Ardo | 0.6 | 140
Belin | 310 | 260
Cerro | 2.1 | 410
Dovan | 95 | 380

On Earth, a single rotation (one day) is far shorter than a full orbit (one year). A student studying the planets of the star Kepra claims that for at least one of these planets, this pattern is reversed, even though most of the planets follow the same pattern as Earth.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?
c: Dovan takes 95 Earth days to rotate once, longer than either Ardo or Cerro takes.
Cerro takes longer to orbit Kepra than any other planet in the table does.
Belin takes 310 Earth days to rotate once but only 260 Earth days to orbit Kepra, whereas Ardo, Cerro, and Dovan each take much less time to rotate than to orbit.
Belin takes 310 Earth days to rotate once, the longest rotation time in the table.
questions.e: The claim has two parts: at least one planet is reversed, and most are not. Only the sentence comparing Belin's 310-day rotation with its 260-day orbit, and contrasting it with the other three planets, supports both parts; the sentence giving Belin's rotation alone never shows the reversal.
ce: It compares rotation times only; Dovan's rotation (95) is still far shorter than its orbit (380).
It uses only the orbit column and shows no reversal.
Correct: it shows one reversed planet (Belin) and that the other three follow Earth's pattern, matching both parts of the claim.
True, but without the orbit time it does not show that Belin's rotation is longer than its year.

questions.p:
Mango deliveries and prices at a city market, by week
Week | Mangoes delivered (thousand kg) | Average price (Egyptian pounds per kg)
1 | 40 | 30
2 | 55 | 26
3 | 70 | 21
4 | 35 | 33

A student claims that, as basic supply-and-demand reasoning would predict, the market's mango price tended to fall when more mangoes arrived and to rise when fewer did.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?
c: As deliveries rose from 40 to 70 thousand kilograms between Weeks 1 and 3, the price fell from 30 to 21 pounds, and when deliveries dropped to 35 thousand kilograms in Week 4, the price rose to 33 pounds.
The highest average price in the table, 33 pounds per kilogram, was recorded in Week 4.
In Week 2, 55 thousand kilograms were delivered at an average price of 26 pounds per kilogram.
Deliveries in Week 4 were lower than in Week 1, and the price in Week 4 was lower than in Week 1.
questions.e: The claim describes a relationship in both directions, so the data must show price falling as deliveries rise (Weeks 1–3) and rising when deliveries fall (Week 4). The choice saying the Week 4 price was lower misreads the table.
ce: Correct: it shows the price falling as supply rose and rising when supply fell, both halves of the claim.
It gives one price without connecting it to deliveries.
One week's data cannot show a pattern of change.
Misreads the table: the Week 4 price (33) was higher than the Week 1 price (30).

questions.p: Ancient Egyptian farmers depended on the Nile's yearly flood, which spread water and fertile silt over their fields. Records kept over many centuries show that when the flood was very low, harvests often failed. Yet when the flood was extremely high, villages were damaged and fields stayed underwater too long to be planted on time. These records suggest that, for Egyptian farmers, ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the best floods were neither the highest nor the lowest but those of a moderate height.
the higher the flood, the larger the harvest that followed.
the flood mattered less to the harvest than the skill of the farmers.
low floods damaged villages more seriously than high floods did.
questions.e: Both extremes caused problems (low floods meant failed harvests; very high floods meant damage and late planting), so moderate floods were best. "The higher the flood, the larger the harvest" ignores the harm done by extremely high floods.
ce: Correct: very low floods caused failed harvests and very high floods caused damage and late planting, so a middle level was best.
Contradicts the text: extremely high floods delayed planting and damaged villages.
The text never discusses farmers' skill; it shows the flood mattered a great deal.
Reversed: the text links village damage to high floods, not low ones.

questions.p: Many theaters sell tickets at a single price for every performance of a play. One small theater instead began charging less for weekday performances, which had often been half empty, and more for Saturday evenings, which had usually sold out weeks in advance. After the change, weekday audiences grew, and Saturday performances still sold out. This outcome suggests that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: demand for Saturday performances was strong enough that the higher prices did not leave seats empty.
the theater lost money on its Saturday performances after the change.
weekday audiences grew because the plays performed on weekdays were better.
most theatergoers prefer weekday performances to Saturday performances.
questions.e: Saturday shows kept selling out after prices went up, which shows that demand for them was strong. The claim that most people prefer weekdays reverses the evidence: weekdays had been half empty until prices were cut.
ce: Correct: Saturday shows still sold out even at higher prices, so demand stayed strong.
Saturday shows sold out at higher prices, so nothing suggests a loss.
The text links the growth to lower prices; it says nothing about the quality of the plays.
Reversed: Saturdays sold out even at higher prices, while weekdays had been half empty.

questions.p: A festival of shadow-puppet theater presented plays from three traditions: karagöz, from ______ wayang kulit, from Indonesia; and tholpavakoothu, from southern India.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Turkey,
Turkey:
Turkey;
Turkey
questions.e: Each item has its own comma ("karagöz, from Turkey"), so the items are separated by semicolons, as after "Indonesia." A comma would make the list confusing, and a second colon cannot separate items.
ce: A comma here would not match the semicolon used between the other items and would blur where each item ends.
A colon has already introduced the list; a second colon cannot separate list items.
Correct: the list items already contain commas, so semicolons separate the items (SAT/ACT extra rule), matching the semicolon after "Indonesia."
With no punctuation, "Turkey wayang kulit" runs two items together.

questions.p: Ibn Daniyal's shadow plays—written in Cairo in the thirteenth ______ are among the oldest surviving scripts for shadow theater in Arabic.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: century,
century;
century
century—
questions.e: "Written in Cairo in the thirteenth century" is extra information that begins with a dash, so it must end with a dash before the verb "are." A comma does not match the opening dash, and a semicolon separates the subject from its verb.
ce: A comma cannot close extra information that opened with a dash; the pair must match.
A semicolon would cut the subject "Ibn Daniyal's shadow plays" off from its verb "are."
Without a closing dash, the extra information never ends.
Correct: the extra information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash.

questions.p: Aryabhata, an Indian mathematician and astronomer, proposed around 499 CE that Earth rotates on its ______ most astronomers of his time continued to assume that the sky itself turned around a motionless Earth.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: axis, however,
axis however,
axis; however
axis; however,
questions.e: Both sides are complete sentences, and "however" is a transition, not a joining word, so it needs a semicolon (or a period) before it and a comma after it. "Axis, however," is the classic comma splice trap.
ce: Comma splice: "however" is not a conjunction, so commas alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Run-on: there is no punctuation to separate the two complete sentences before "however."
"However" at the start of a clause must be followed by a comma.
Correct: a semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and "however" is followed by a comma.

questions.p: The best-known writer of Japan's Noh ______ Zeami Motokiyo, also wrote treatises on the art of acting that are still read today.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: theater,
theater
theater—
theater;
questions.e: The comma after "Motokiyo" closes the name, so a matching comma must open it: "The best-known writer of Japan's Noh theater, Zeami Motokiyo, also wrote…" A dash would not match, and a semicolon makes a fragment.
ce: Correct: the name is extra information that ends with a comma after "Motokiyo," so it must open with a matching comma.
Without an opening comma, the comma after "Motokiyo" separates the subject from its verb "wrote."
A dash cannot open extra information that closes with a comma; the pair must match.
A semicolon would leave "The best-known writer of Japan's Noh theater" as a fragment.

questions.p: Among the objects found in the ruins of the medieval caravanserai ______ a set of bronze weights, a pair of balance scales, and a clay jar still holding traces of pepper.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: was
were
is
has been
questions.e: In this inverted sentence the subject comes after the verb: "a set …, a pair …, and a clay jar." Three items joined by "and" make a plural subject, so "were" is correct; "was" is the trap of agreeing with a nearby singular noun.
ce: Singular: it agrees with "caravanserai" or "ruins" instead of the plural subject after the verb.
Correct: the sentence is inverted, and the real subject that follows is plural (weights, scales, and a jar), so "were" is needed.
Singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the find happened in the past.
Singular verb that does not agree with the three-part subject.

questions.p: Written in the tenth century, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: al-Mutanabbi wrote poems that are still memorized and quoted across the Arab world.
al-Mutanabbi's poems are still memorized and quoted across the Arab world.
readers across the Arab world still memorize and quote al-Mutanabbi's poems.
there are poems by al-Mutanabbi that are still memorized and quoted across the Arab world.
questions.e: The opening phrase "Written in the tenth century" must describe the noun right after the comma, and only the poems were written. Putting "al-Mutanabbi" or "readers" there makes it seem that the poet or the readers were written.
ce: Dangling modifier: this says that al-Mutanabbi himself was "written in the tenth century."
Correct: the poems were written in the tenth century, so "poems" must come right after the opening phrase.
Dangling modifier: this says the readers were written in the tenth century.
"There" cannot be the thing that was written; the modifier has nothing to describe.

questions.p: In one medieval city, members of the merchants' guild met each spring to check the standard weights used in the market. Any trader found using false weights ______ fined, and repeat offenders could be banned from the market.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: were
was
have been
being
questions.e: The subject is "Any trader" (singular), and the passage is in the past, so "was" is correct. "Were" agrees with the nearby noun "weights," and "being" leaves the clause without a finite verb.
ce: Plural verb; the subject is "Any trader," not "weights."
Correct: the subject "Any trader" is singular, and the past tense matches "met" and "could be banned."
Plural and present perfect; it agrees with neither the subject nor the past time frame.
Not a finite verb, so the clause would have no main verb.

questions.p: For centuries, many thinkers assumed that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones. Experiments in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries challenged this view: when air resistance is small, objects of very different weights fall at nearly the same rate. ______ a feather does fall more slowly than a stone in ordinary air, because the air pushes back far more strongly on the feather's large, light surface.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Admittedly,
Therefore,
For this reason,
Specifically,
questions.e: After stating that objects fall at nearly the same rate, the writer concedes an everyday case that seems to contradict it, so "Admittedly" fits. "Therefore" and "For this reason" wrongly present the slow feather as a consequence of equal falling rates.
ce: Correct: the last sentence concedes a case that seems to support the old view, then explains it.
The feather falling slowly is not a result of objects falling at the same rate; it seems to go against it.
The slow feather is not caused by the experiments' finding; it is caused by air resistance.
The feather does not give more detail about equal falling rates; it is an apparent exception.

questions.p: Economists distinguish between goods whose prices are set in open markets and goods whose prices are fixed by governments. In the first case, prices can change daily as supply and demand shift. ______ in the second case, prices may stay the same for years, even when shortages or surpluses develop.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: By contrast,
Consequently,
Similarly,
For example,
questions.e: The passage sets two cases side by side, prices that change daily and prices that stay fixed for years, so "By contrast" fits. "Similarly" ignores the difference, and "Consequently" invents a cause-and-effect link.
ce: Correct: unchanging fixed prices are set against prices that change daily.
Fixed prices staying the same is not caused by market prices changing daily.
The two cases are different, not similar.
The second case is not an example of the first; it is the other case.

questions.p: Movable type was invented in China around 1040, roughly four centuries before printing with movable type began in Europe. ______ it did not replace woodblock printing in China for many centuries; because written Chinese uses thousands of different characters, carving whole pages onto wooden blocks often remained simpler and cheaper.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: As a result,
Similarly,
In other words,
Even so,
questions.e: An invention four centuries ahead of Europe might be expected to spread quickly, but it did not, so the concession "Even so" fits. "As a result" is wrong because the reason given for woodblock printing's survival is the number of characters, not the early invention.
ce: The early invention did not cause woodblock printing to survive; the number of characters did.
Nothing similar is being added; the sentence contrasts with what an early invention might lead us to expect.
The second sentence does not restate the first; it adds a surprising limitation.
Correct: despite its early invention, movable type did not take over, which is an unexpected contrast.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tawfiq al-Hakim (1898–1987) was an Egyptian playwright and novelist.
• His play The People of the Cave was published in 1933.
• It retells the story of sleepers who wake after centuries and find the world changed.
• Critics often describe it as a landmark in the development of modern Arabic drama.
questions.q: The student wants to present The People of the Cave and explain its importance. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The People of the Cave retells the story of sleepers who wake after centuries and find the world changed.
Tawfiq al-Hakim, who lived from 1898 to 1987, was an Egyptian playwright and novelist.
Tawfiq al-Hakim's 1933 play The People of the Cave, which retells the story of sleepers who wake after centuries, is often described by critics as a landmark of modern Arabic drama.
Critics often describe some Egyptian plays as landmarks in the development of modern Arabic drama.
questions.e: The goal has two parts, presenting the play and explaining its importance, and only the sentence calling the 1933 play "a landmark of modern Arabic drama" does both. The plot summary presents the play but leaves out its importance.
ce: It summarizes the plot but says nothing about the play's importance.
It introduces the writer but does not present the play or its importance.
Correct: it presents the play (author, date, story) and gives its importance (a landmark).
It never names the play, so it does not present it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990.
• It orbits Earth about 540 kilometers above the surface.
• The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in December 2021.
• It operates about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
• Webb observes mainly infrared light, while Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a difference in where the two telescopes operate. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Webb observes mainly infrared light, while Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, and the James Webb Space Telescope was launched in December 2021.
While the Hubble Space Telescope orbits Earth about 540 kilometers above the surface, the James Webb Space Telescope operates about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
The James Webb Space Telescope operates about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
questions.e: The goal is a difference in location, so the sentence must set Hubble's 540-kilometer orbit against Webb's position 1.5 million kilometers away. The light-type sentence is the trap: it is a difference, but not the one the goal names.
ce: This is a real difference, but it is about the light they observe, not where they operate.
This contrasts launch dates, not locations.
Correct: it contrasts the locations of the two telescopes, which is the difference the goal asks for.
It gives one telescope's location only, so it shows no difference.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In a descending-price auction, the price starts high and falls step by step.
• The first bidder to stop the falling price buys the goods at that price.
• The method is used at large flower auctions in the Netherlands.
• It allows many lots to be sold very quickly.
questions.q: The student wants to explain how a descending-price auction decides who buys the goods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Descending-price auctions are used at large flower auctions in the Netherlands.
In a descending-price auction, the price starts high and falls step by step until one bidder stops it, and that bidder buys the goods at that price.
A descending-price auction allows many lots to be sold very quickly.
In a descending-price auction, the price starts high and falls step by step.
questions.e: To explain who buys, the sentence must include the deciding rule: the first bidder to stop the falling price wins at that price. The sentence that only describes the falling price leaves out the rule, and the other two give place and speed.
ce: It says where the method is used, not how the buyer is decided.
Correct: it explains the process and states who becomes the buyer.
It gives an advantage, not the rule for deciding the buyer.
It describes the falling price but never says who buys the goods.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the reasons for EVERY question, including the ones you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason and not by luck.
For each mistake, write three things in your notebook: the skill tag, the trap that caught you (too broad, reversed, half-right, comma splice, and so on), and the rule or step you will use next time.
Look at your results by skill. Any skill below 80% appears under "Study these again" with a link to its lesson.

Go back to the matching lessons: Words in Context; High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs; Semicolons; Colons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronoun Case and Sound-Alike Pronouns; Verb Tense and Aspect; Verb Finiteness; Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).
Do the practice sets on each of those lesson pages, then take Practice Test 5 under the same timed conditions.
